_about: Round 1's log rules (docs/specs/round-1.md#signals). Read by terraform/modules/alerts and kql/backtest.py. Each rule runs its file with these parameters prepended as KQL let statements, after the environment's targets (Servers, Apps, Gateway, TargetEnv, TargetDatabaseId) and the time range (Start = ago(lookback), End = now()). Values are KQL literals. Round 2: "envs" lists the environments a rule exists in (default both), "enabled_in" those where it runs outside drills. Round 3: "backtest_params" override params in backtests only (the SLO rules report every step there). S4: "about" and "first_steps" are the rule's description in Azure, shown on its Teams card (docs/specs/round-3.md#incident-response); they name no repo path, server, app or person. Round 4: L1-wait also reads the job's "lock_wait" rows; E1 tickets deploys and entrypoint warnings.

L1-wait.title: Lock wait over 60 s
L1-wait.about: A statement on the Odoo database waited over 60 s for a lock. Each waiting web request holds one Odoo worker; when all are held the health probe fails and Azure kills the container, and every user in flight gets a 502 (2026-08-20: 84, then 113).
first_steps: Open in Azure: the row gives the server and the longest wait.
In the server's Postgres log, read the lines just before: the waiting process, the process holding the lock, and both statements.
Check the same minutes for 5xx (L2) and restarts (M1, M2) on the apps.
If waits continue or users see 502s: call the ERP team with the holding process and its statement. Ending a session is their call; the track only reads.

L1-burst.title: Burst of lock waits or lock timeouts
L1-burst.about: More than 40 lock waits, or more than 12 statements cancelled by the 10 s lock timeout, in 5 minutes, or a request Odoo failed after its 5 tries: contention is stalling work. A cancelled web request is retried by Odoo, background work by its own job; Failed above 0 means a user saw an error (usual level: 3 to 4 cancellations per 5 minutes).
first_steps: Open in Azure: the row gives the server and the counts; Failed above 0 means a user saw an error.
In the server's Postgres log, group the waits and cancellations by relation: one table or one task usually dominates.
Check the scheduled tasks and queue jobs running at that time (an import, a bulk update, a cleanup).
Next working day: send the table, the counts and the times to the ERP team.

L2-5xx.title: HTTP 5xx burst
L2-5xx.about: 25 or more requests answered 5xx in 5 minutes. A burst of 502 means the app had no backend (a container killed or starting); 500 means Odoo answered with its own error (2026-08-20 evening: every TV poll got 500 after a deploy).
first_steps: Look at the codes on the row: 502 or 500, and which app.
502: check the app's system log for a ProbeFailure kill or a restart in the same minutes, and lock waits (L1).
500: check the app's revisions for a deploy in the last hour, and Odoo's console lines for the error.
Call the ERP team with the codes, the paths and any deploy time; a rollback is theirs.

L2-499.title: HTTP 499 burst (users gave up)
L2-499.about: 25 or more requests in 5 minutes where the user gave up before an answer: pages slow enough that people leave. It often comes just before a 502 burst (2026-08-20 03:05: 39 users gave up, then the container was killed).
first_steps: Open in Azure: the app and the count.
Check the same minutes for 502s (L2-5xx), lock waits (L1) and a busy database (M3, Q1).
Find the slowest paths in the nginx lines of that window.
Next working day: the paths and times to the ERP team.

L3.title: VPN tunnel down
L3.about: A VPN tunnel to on-prem has been down over 5 minutes and is still down. Imports from the on-prem SQL Server stop and their queue jobs fail (2026-09-21: down 6.7 h).
first_steps: Open in Azure: which gateway instance, and since when (the other instance may still be up).
In the gateway's IKE log, read the error codes around the drop (L4).
Watch failed queue jobs (L5) for the sync models.
Call the platform team; the on-prem side (the firewall, the peer) is the on-prem team's.

L4.title: IKE negotiation errors
L4.about: An IKE negotiation of the VPN ended with an error code. Usually a rekey that heals by itself; repeated or new codes have come before outages (13805 in 2026-08, 13885 on 2026-09-11).
first_steps: Open in Azure: the code and the time.
Check the tunnel's state now (L3) and the count of the same code over the last day.
If the code is new or repeats every hour, check failed sync jobs (L5).
Next working day: the codes and their rhythm to the platform team.

L5-page.title: Job queue backlog
L5-page.about: The job queue is behind: jobs ready to run have waited over 60 minutes in 2 or more channels (or 500 in one), or over 5,000 jobs are pending (the Check field says which: behind or pending). Imports from on-prem stop reaching Odoo (2026-08-25: 60,696 pending overnight; 2026-11-10: 865 sync jobs waited 2 h). One late channel alone is L5-ticket's stall.
first_steps: Open the results: Detail lists each late channel, its ready jobs, their wait and the running job's minutes.
Is the cron app running its jobs? Check its restarts (M2), kills (L7) and worker ends (O1).
Is the tunnel up (L3)? Most jobs read the on-prem SQL Server.
Call the ERP team with the check, the late channels and since when.

L5-ticket.title: Job queue failures, stall or size
L5-ticket.about: A job queue problem for the ERP team (the Check field says which): failed, over 10 failed jobs of one model in the last hour; stall, one channel's ready jobs waited over 60 minutes in the last 24 h; dead, jobs whose worker ended mid-run in the last 24 h (JobFoundDead; since 2026-11-10 on the endpoint imports); size, queue_job over 2.5 GB. Stall and dead stay open a day after the last case, so one cause makes one ticket.
first_steps: Open the results: Check, the value and Detail (the model, or the channel and its running job).
Failed or dead: read those jobs in Odoo (Queue Jobs, state Failed; JobFoundDead means the worker ended mid-run).
Stall: in Queue Jobs, filter on the channel: a started job with a climbing retry is dying and being re-run.
Size: check that the cleanup of done jobs still runs (L6).
Next working day: the check, the model or channel and the times to the ERP team.

L6.title: Late scheduled tasks
L6.about: An Odoo scheduled task is overdue by more than its interval plus 30 minutes (at least 60 minutes). Its work has stopped, silently (2026-11-04: the daily Auto-vacuum task stopped; still open).
first_steps: Open in Azure: the task, how late, its last and next run.
In Odoo (Scheduled Actions), check that the task is active and when it last ran.
Check the cron app is up (M2, L7) and the queue is moving (L5).
Next working day: the task to the ERP team (they may have stopped it on purpose).

L7.title: App container killed or crash looping
L7.about: An app's container died: killed out of memory (exit 137), exited 3 or more times in 15 minutes with 2 or more restarts (a crash loop; a single restart is M1, M2's ticket), or killed by Azure 2 or more times after failed health probes (every worker busy). Users of the web app get 502s while it restarts.
first_steps: Look at the row: the app, and which count (OomKills, Exited with Restarts, ProbeKills).
ProbeKills: check lock waits (L1) and long requests just before each kill (the 2026-08-20 pattern).
OomKills or Exited: read the app's last console lines before each exit, and its memory.
Call the ERP team with the app, the times and the last lines; a restart or a resize is theirs.

E1.title: A deploy or an entrypoint warning on an Odoo app
E1.about: An Odoo app got a new revision (a deploy), or its entrypoint printed a WARNING at a container start (a configuration check that failed: 2026-08-20 to 09-23, the memory limit above the container's, read by nobody for 34 days). A deploy is information beside the other cards; a warning is for the ERP team.
first_steps: Look at the row: Revisions (a deploy) or Warnings, and the app.
A deploy: note its time; if pages follow within the hour (L2, L7, SLO), name the deploy when calling the ERP team.
A warning: read the line on the card and send it to the ERP team; the configuration is theirs.
Nothing to do on the platform: the track only reads.

H.title: SQL job heartbeat missing
H.about: No heartbeat from the track's SQL job in 30 minutes: the job failed, could not reach the database, or could not write to the workspace. While it is missing, L5, L6 and T1 see nothing.
first_steps: Check the job's last runs and their state in the job's execution history.
A failed run: read its console log (database login, network, or ingestion refused).
If the database is unreachable, check the server is alive (M5).
The job and its role are the track's own: fix it; tell the platform team if the server is the cause.

Q1.title: Heavy hour on the Odoo database
Q1.about: The Odoo database used over 90 minutes of query time in one hour (the usual hour is under 69). The row names the 3 costliest query ids.
first_steps: Open in Azure: the hour and the 3 query ids.
Look the ids up in Query Store (the query text is on the server, not in the workspace).
Check what ran that hour: imports, reports, a bulk task.
Next working day: the ids, their text and the hour to the ERP team.

T1.title: Table bloat autovacuum is losing
T1.about: A table has 25 % or more dead rows, at least 100,000, and no autovacuum for 24 hours: autovacuum is losing, and the table and its queries grow slower.
first_steps: Open in Azure: the table, its dead rows and its last autovacuum.
Check long-open transactions on the server (they stop the cleanup).
Check the table's write rate: a bulk update or a task looping.
Next working day: to the platform team (vacuum settings) and the ERP team (the writer).

O1.title: Odoo workers at their limits
O1.about: Odoo stated 3 or more worker ends in 15 minutes: a memory or CPU limit reached, a timeout, or a critical worker error. Requests in flight on those workers fail.
first_steps: Open in Azure: the count by kind (memory_limit, cpu_limit, timeout, critical).
Memory or CPU: find the request or task the worker was running in Odoo's log lines before each end.
Timeout: check lock waits (L1) and the database's load (M3).
Call the ERP team with the kinds, the times and the requests.

R1.title: View refresh over its budget
R1.about: A refresh of the dev view lot_stock_view ran longer than 300 s, its 5-minute schedule: refreshes start to overlap and load the dev server (2026-09-09: up to 28 minutes).
first_steps: Open in Azure: the refresh's duration.
Check the dev server's CPU and whether two refreshes overlap.
Next working day: to the ERP team (the schedule or the view's query).

SLO-fast.title: Error budget burning fast (2 % of 30 days' budget in 1 h)
SLO-fast.about: This journey (tv or interactive) is spending its 30-day error budget over 14.4 times too fast, in the last hour and the last 5 minutes: at this pace 2 % of the month's budget goes in an hour. Users are failing now.
first_steps: Look at the Journey and the burn on the row.
Find the failing paths and codes in the web app's nginx lines of the last hour (L2 shows the codes).
Check the web app for a deploy, kills or restarts in that hour.
Call the ERP team; if users are blocked, tell the business channel what fails and when the next update comes.

SLO-slow.title: Error budget burning steadily (5 % of 30 days' budget in 6 h)
SLO-slow.about: This journey is spending its error budget 6 times too fast over 6 hours and the last 30 minutes: a slow leak of failures that never makes a burst.
first_steps: Look at the Journey and the burn on the row.
Group the last 6 hours' 5xx by path: one endpoint usually dominates.
Check for a recent deploy or a failing scheduled task behind that path.
Next working day: the path and its error to the ERP team.
